title: Stack, Heap and Memory Allocation
objectives: Say what lives on a thread’s stack and what lives on the heap
Explain what an allocator does between your program and the kernel
Recognise fragmentation and choose arenas or pools for short-lived objects

cards.title: Two places a value can live
cards.body: Each thread has a stack: a contiguous region where every function call pushes a frame holding its locals and return address, and every return pops it. Allocating there is just moving a pointer, and it is freed automatically on return, but the size is fixed when the thread starts (commonly 1 to 8 MB, depending on the platform and settings). The heap is shared by all threads and holds data of any size whose lifetime is not tied to one call; an allocator has to find space for it and take it back later.

cards.title: Worked example: how deep can recursion go?
cards.body: A recursive walk is fine on a balanced tree and crashes on a degenerate one.
steps: Assume an 8 MB stack (8,388,608 bytes) and 200-byte frames (illustrative)
Frames that fit: 8,388,608 ÷ 200 ≈ 41,900 nested calls
A balanced tree of 1 million nodes is about 20 levels deep: 20 frames, no problem
A degenerate tree (a linked list in disguise) of 1 million nodes needs 1 million frames, about 200 MB: the thread runs into the guard page below its stack and the process gets a segmentation fault
Fix: replace recursion with a loop and an explicit stack stored on the heap, which can grow to any size

cards.title: What sits between malloc and the kernel
cards.body: An allocator asks the kernel for large regions (by moving the program break or mapping pages) and carves them into blocks. Most allocators round small requests up to a size class, keep free lists per class, and give each thread a small cache so common allocations need no lock. Very large requests are usually mapped directly and handed back to the kernel when freed; small freed blocks normally stay inside the process for reuse.

cards.title: Misconception: freeing memory shrinks the process
cards.body: After a program frees most of its objects, its resident memory often stays near the peak. The allocator keeps freed small blocks for the next request, and it can only return a page to the kernel when every block on it is free. Resident size is therefore a high-water mark shaped by the allocator, not a live count of the data in use.

cards.title: Trap: fragmentation in a process that runs for weeks
cards.body: When objects of many sizes and lifetimes are mixed, freed blocks leave holes between long-lived ones. Total free space can be large while no single hole fits the next request, so the allocator asks the kernel for more and resident memory creeps up with no leak in the code. Group objects that die together in an arena or pool, reuse buffers of fixed sizes, and compare live data with resident memory before hunting for a leak.

questions.prompt: A function fills a local array and returns a pointer to it. Callers sometimes see garbage. Why?

choices.label: The heap allocator frees local arrays as the function exits
The array was in the returned function’s frame, which later calls reuse
The kernel unmaps that stack page as soon as the call returns
Local arrays become read-only once their function has returned

questions.explanation: Locals live in the function’s stack frame; after the return that memory is reused by the next call, so the pointer now aims at whatever is written there. The heap allocator never manages locals, the kernel does not unmap stack pages on every return (the stack region stays mapped), and nothing makes the memory read-only. Return a heap allocation or let the caller pass in the buffer.

questions.prompt: A batch job frees 2 GB of small objects at the end of each run, yet its resident memory stays near the 2.5 GB peak. What is the usual reason?

choices.label: Freed blocks stay in the allocator for reuse
Freed pages move into the page cache but stay counted as the process’s
The kernel zeroes freed pages slowly, a batch at a time
The stack keeps a copy of every object the job allocated

questions.explanation: Allocators keep small freed blocks in their free lists and can return a page only when all of it is free, so resident memory behaves like a high-water mark. Heap pages do not turn into page cache, zeroing is not what holds them, and stacks hold frames, not copies of heap objects.

questions.prompt: Live data stays at 1 GB, but over a week resident memory climbs from 1.2 GB to 3 GB. Heap profiles show no growing object type. Which explanation fits?

choices.label: The main thread’s stack grows a little with each request
Log files read by the process count as its resident heap
Freed holes are too small or scattered to reuse
The translation buffer keeps more entries as uptime grows

questions.explanation: Fragmentation grows resident memory without growing live data: free space exists but in pieces that do not fit new requests. Stacks are fixed-size and reused, cached file pages are not part of the heap, and the TLB is a small fixed-size CPU cache that has nothing to do with resident memory.

questions.prompt: A recursive tree walk works on balanced trees but crashes with a segmentation fault on a 1-million-node degenerate tree. What is the robust fix?

choices.label: Catch the fault and retry the walk on a fresh thread
Split the walk across more threads running at once
Raise the heap size limit for the process
Use a loop with an explicit stack kept on the heap

questions.explanation: The crash is stack exhaustion: one frame per level, a million levels. A heap-allocated work stack grows as needed. Retrying overflows again, more threads each have their own small stack and the walk is still deep, and the heap limit does not affect the thread’s stack size. Raising the stack size also works but only moves the limit.

questions.prompt: A thread’s stack is 1 MB (1,048,576 bytes) and each recursive call uses a 256-byte frame. About how many nested calls fit?
assumptions: The whole stack is available for these frames
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a few thousand levels is plenty for balanced structures (a billion-node balanced tree is about 30 deep) but not for input-shaped recursion such as a long linked list or deeply nested JSON from users.

questions.prompt: Order what a typical allocator does for a small allocation, from the cheapest path to the most expensive.

items.label: If the cache is empty, refill it from the shared free lists under a lock
Round the size up to its size class
If those are empty too, ask the kernel for more pages
Take a free block from this thread’s cache for that class

questions.explanation: Size class, then the lock-free thread cache, then the shared lists, then a system call; most allocations stop at the second step.

flashcards.back: Stack: per thread, frames freed on return, fixed size. Heap: shared, any size and lifetime, managed by an allocator.

flashcards.front: Why doesn’t resident memory drop after free?
flashcards.back: Allocators keep freed blocks for reuse and can return a page only when all of it is free.
Free memory split into holes that do not fit new requests, so the process grows without a leak.

mechanism.title: How memory is handed out inside a process
steps: A thread’s stack is reserved when the thread starts. The main thread’s size usually comes from a resource limit (RLIMIT_STACK, often 8 MB on Linux); other threads get a size chosen by the thread library or the caller. An unmapped guard page sits below it, so running off the end faults immediately instead of silently overwriting other memory.

Each call pushes a frame with arguments that do not fit in registers, saved registers, locals and the return address. Allocation and freeing are a single pointer adjustment, which is why stack data is effectively free, and why it cannot outlive the call that created it.

The heap is managed by an allocator library in user space. It obtains memory from the kernel in large chunks, splits it into size classes (for example 16, 32, 48 bytes and up), and keeps free lists for each. Per-thread caches serve most requests without locks; only refills and returns touch shared structures.

Large blocks follow a different path: above a threshold (128 KB by default in the GNU C library, adjusted dynamically) allocations are mapped directly from the kernel and unmapped on free, so they return memory at once. Small blocks are carved out of shared regions and return memory only when whole pages or the top of the heap become free.

Fragmentation is the gap between the memory a process holds and the memory its live objects need. External fragmentation is free space split into unusable holes; internal fragmentation is space wasted by rounding a request up to its size class, such as a 33-byte request in a 48-byte class.

Arenas (also called regions or bump allocators) serve a group of objects that die together, such as everything built while handling one request: allocation is a pointer bump and the whole arena is reset at once. Pools of fixed-size objects avoid fragmentation for one hot type. Garbage-collected runtimes solve the same problem differently, often by moving live objects together.

useWhen: Use the stack for small, call-scoped data and the heap for anything large or longer-lived.
Use arenas or pools when many objects share a lifetime or a size.
avoidWhen: Avoid recursion whose depth is set by user input.
Avoid reading resident memory alone as proof of a leak; compare it with live data.

rows: Nothing inside can outlive the arena
One size per pool; idle memory stays reserved

numbers.title: What a per-request arena saves
assumptions: 10,000 requests a second, each making 2,000 small allocations that all die when the request ends (illustrative)
About 50 ns per malloc and free pair on a general-purpose allocator and about 2 ns per arena bump (illustrative orders of magnitude)
steps: Allocations: 10,000 × 2,000 = 20 million a second.
General allocator: 20,000,000 × 50 ns = 1.0 CPU-second per second, a whole core spent on allocation.
Arena: 20,000,000 × 2 ns = 0.04 CPU-seconds per second, plus one reset per request.
Freeing is free with the arena, and because each request reuses the same memory, fragmentation from these objects disappears.
numbers.result: For short-lived, same-lifetime objects an arena turns about one core of allocator work into about 4% of a core; measure your own allocator before assuming the gap.

india.title: How one C library returns memory to the kernel
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The mallopt(3) manual page documents the GNU C library allocator’s thresholds. Requests at or above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KB by default, adjusted dynamically) are served with mmap, which the page notes has the advantage that such blocks can always be released back to the system independently. Smaller blocks come from the heap, which is trimmed only from its top when more than M_TRIM_THRESHOLD bytes are free there, which is why a few long-lived small objects can pin a large heap in place.

pitfalls.trap: “Memory didn’t drop after we freed everything, so we have a leak.”
pitfalls.say: “Allocators keep freed blocks; I’d compare live heap size with resident memory to tell a leak from fragmentation.”

pitfalls.trap: “Recursion is fine, the stack is huge.”
pitfalls.say: “It is a few MB per thread; if input controls the depth I’d use an explicit heap-allocated stack.”

takeaways: Stacks are per thread, fixed in size and freed on return.
Allocators keep freed small blocks, so resident memory is a high-water mark.
Fragmentation grows a process without a leak.
Arenas and pools make same-lifetime or same-size objects cheap.

interactive.title: Speed up an allocation-heavy parser
interactive.prompt: A service parses each 50 KB request body into thousands of tiny objects and drops them all when the response is sent. A profile shows 30% of CPU inside malloc and free. Which change removes the most of that cost?

choices.label: Allocate the request’s objects from a per-request arena and reset it after the response
choices.feedback: Right: allocation becomes a pointer bump and freeing is one reset for the whole request.

choices.label: Give every worker thread a larger stack
choices.feedback: The objects live on the heap; stack size does not change what malloc costs.

choices.label: Add more worker threads so allocation runs in parallel
choices.feedback: More threads multiply the allocator work and can add contention on shared free lists.

interactive.reveal: Objects that are born and die together are the ideal case for an arena: no per-object free, no fragmentation, and allocation cost close to zero. The catch is discipline: nothing built in the arena may be kept after the reset.

title: Garbage Collection: Throughput, Pauses and Heap Size
objectives: Explain how a tracing collector decides what is garbage
Relate allocation rate, live data and heap size to how often collections run
Choose between throughput and pause time, and read a pause’s effect on tail latency

cards.title: Reachable means alive
cards.body: A tracing garbage collector starts from roots (thread stacks, registers and globals), follows every reference it finds, and marks what it reaches. Anything unmarked can never be used again, so its memory is reclaimed. The program never calls free; the price is that the collector must periodically do this work, and at some points it must stop or coordinate with the program’s threads to get a consistent picture.

cards.title: Why most collectors split the heap by age
cards.body: In typical programs most objects die young: request buffers, temporary strings, iterators. A generational collector allocates into a small young area and collects it often; survivors are copied into an older area that is collected rarely. Copying only the few survivors is cheap, so young collections cost roughly in proportion to live data, not to garbage.

cards.title: Worked example: heap size sets the collection rate
cards.body: Headroom above live data is what the allocator can fill before the next collection.
steps: A service allocates 500 MB/s and keeps 1 GB of live data (illustrative)
With a 2 GB heap the headroom is 1 GB: a collection every 1 GB ÷ 500 MB/s = 2 s
With a 4 GB heap the headroom is 3 GB: a collection every 6 s, three times less often
Each collection still has to trace about the same 1 GB of live data, so total GC work per second falls about threefold
Below about 1.2 GB the headroom approaches zero and the process collects almost continuously, then fails with out-of-memory

cards.title: Trap: a heap limit larger than the container
cards.body: A runtime that sizes its heap from the machine’s memory, or a heap flag copied from a bigger host, can let the heap grow past the container’s memory limit. The collector sees plenty of room and defers work, then the kernel kills the process for exceeding its cgroup limit, with no out-of-memory error from the runtime at all. Set the heap limit below the container limit, leaving room for thread stacks, native buffers and the runtime itself.

cards.title: Misconception: a concurrent collector has no cost
cards.body: Concurrent collectors do most marking while the program runs, so pauses shrink to milliseconds. The work does not vanish: they spend CPU on background threads, add small checks (barriers) to reference writes or reads, and need extra headroom because the program keeps allocating during a cycle. If allocation outruns the collector, it falls back to a long stop-the-world collection.

questions.prompt: Objects X and Y point at each other, and no stack frame or global variable refers to either. Under a tracing collector, what happens to the pair?

choices.label: Keeps both, since each still has a reference count of one
Frees both, because neither can be reached from a root
Frees one and keeps the other to preserve a single reference
Moves both into the old generation for a later decision

questions.explanation: Tracing works from roots, so a cycle that no root reaches is garbage no matter how its members point at each other. Keeping them because of a nonzero count is how plain reference counting behaves, which is exactly why it leaks cycles. Freeing only one is not a rule any collector uses, and promotion depends on surviving collections, not on cycles.

questions.prompt: Why is a young-generation collection usually fast even when the young area was full of objects?

choices.label: Young objects are smaller, so tracing each one costs less
The young area is collected only when the program is idle
Its cost tracks the few survivors, not the dead objects
Young collections skip the roots and scan the heap linearly

questions.explanation: A copying young collection touches only what is still alive; dead objects are reclaimed by reusing the whole area. Object size matters little, collections run when the young area fills rather than when idle, and roots are always where tracing begins.

questions.prompt: A service collects every 0.5 seconds and spends 25% of CPU in the collector. Live data is steady at 1.8 GB in a 2 GB heap. What is the best first step?

choices.label: Raise the heap limit to give real headroom above live data
Call the collector by hand after every request
Add more collector threads and keep the heap size
Lower the young area so each collection has less to do

questions.explanation: With 0.2 GB of headroom the program fills it almost immediately, so collections run back to back, each tracing 1.8 GB. More headroom spaces them out. Collecting by hand adds collections, more threads spread the same excess work, and a smaller young area makes collections even more frequent.

questions.prompt: A service has a 150 ms p99 target. The collector pauses for 200 ms about every 10 seconds, and requests take 20 ms otherwise. Which effect should you expect?

choices.label: No effect on p99, since pauses are rare compared with requests
Only the request running during the pause is slowed
About 2% of requests are delayed, so p99 breaks the target
The p50 rises to about 200 ms while the p99 stays fine

questions.explanation: Requests arriving during a 200 ms window out of every 10 s, about 2% of them, wait up to 200 ms, which is more than 1% of traffic, so the 99th percentile falls inside the delayed group. All requests in flight or arriving are delayed, not one, and the median is unaffected because 98% of requests miss the pause.

questions.prompt: A service allocates 400 MB/s, live data is 1.2 GB, and the heap limit is 3.2 GB. Roughly how many seconds pass between collections?
assumptions: Collections start when the heap is full
Live data stays constant
questions.explanation: Design implication: only the headroom above live data buys time, so doubling a heap that is mostly live data can multiply the interval many times over, while the same doubling on a mostly empty heap barely matters.

questions.prompt: Choose a collector setup for a payments API.
constraints: 16 GB heap with 6 GB of live data
Spare CPU of about 20% on each node

approaches.label: A low-pause concurrent collector
approaches.description: Marks while the program runs; pauses of a few milliseconds

approaches.label: A throughput collector
approaches.description: Stops the program for each collection; least total CPU spent

approaches.label: Disable collection and restart nodes nightly
approaches.description: Avoids all collections until memory runs out

rationaleOptions.label: Pauses must stay well below the 50 ms target
The spare CPU can pay for background marking and barriers
Throughput collectors use the least CPU, so they are best here
Restarts remove the need for headroom

rationaleConflicts.r3: Least CPU matters less than pauses that can exceed 50 ms when tracing a large heap stop-the-world.
rationaleConflicts.r4: At normal allocation rates 16 GB fills in minutes, not a day, so the process would run out long before the restart.

questions.explanation: The binding constraint is tail latency, and the node has CPU to spare, so trading CPU for short pauses is the right exchange. A throughput collector is the right choice for batch jobs where only total time counts.

flashcards.front: What does a tracing GC keep?
flashcards.back: Everything reachable from roots (stacks, registers, globals); the rest is garbage, cycles included.
(heap limit − live data) ÷ allocation rate.
Throughput: least CPU, longer stop-the-world pauses. Low-pause: short pauses, more CPU and headroom.

mechanism.title: What a collector does during one cycle
steps: Allocation is a pointer bump in a thread-local buffer inside the young area, so creating an object is about as cheap as using a stack. When the young area fills, a young collection is triggered.

The collector finds roots: references held in every thread’s stack frames and registers and in global variables. To read thread stacks consistently, threads are brought to safe points, which is the part of a pause that grows with the number of threads.

Marking follows references from the roots. References from old objects into the young area are tracked by a write barrier (a small check on each reference store), so a young collection does not need to scan the whole old area.

Survivors are copied into a survivor area or promoted to the old generation after surviving several collections, and the young area is reused from empty. Its cost depends on survivors, which is why short-lived garbage is nearly free.

Old-generation collections are rarer and larger. Concurrent collectors mark the old area while the program runs and compact it piece by piece; throughput collectors stop all threads and do it in parallel, which finishes sooner but pauses longer.
If the program allocates faster than a concurrent cycle can reclaim, or headroom runs out, the collector falls back to a full stop-the-world collection, often the longest pause the service ever sees.

useWhen: Use a throughput collector for batch jobs where only total run time matters.
Use a low-pause collector when tail latency has a target and the node has CPU to spare.
avoidWhen: Avoid running with the heap barely above live data; collections become constant.
Avoid heap limits at or above the container memory limit.

rows: Short young pauses, rare longer ones
Tight latency targets on large heaps
None, but cascading frees can stall
Deterministic cleanup; cycles need extra handling

numbers.title: How heap size changes GC cost
assumptions: Allocation of 1.2 GB/s, 1.5 GB of live data (illustrative)
Each collection costs about the same because it traces the same live data
steps: 2 GB heap: headroom 0.5 GB, so a collection every 0.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.42 s, about 2.4 a second.
4 GB heap: headroom 2.5 GB, so a collection every 2.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 2.1 s, about 0.48 a second.
Ratio: 2.4 ÷ 0.48 = 5 times fewer collections for twice the memory.
If one collection costs 100 ms of CPU, GC drops from about 240 ms to about 48 ms of CPU per second.
numbers.result: Doubling the heap here cuts collector CPU about fivefold because headroom grows from 0.5 GB to 2.5 GB; memory is the cheapest GC tuning knob when live data is close to the limit.

india.title: Generations in a managed runtime
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s documentation for the .NET garbage collector describes three generations. Generation 0 holds short-lived objects such as temporary variables and is collected most frequently; objects that survive move to generation 1, a buffer between short- and long-lived objects, and then to generation 2 for long-lived data. Because a collection can release memory in one generation rather than across the whole managed heap, most collections stay small and fast, which is the same idea used by most generational collectors.

pitfalls.trap: “We have GC pauses, so let’s call the collector manually.”
pitfalls.say: “Manual collections add work; I’d first check headroom above live data and the allocation rate.”

pitfalls.trap: “Average latency is fine, so GC isn’t a problem.”
pitfalls.say: “Pauses hit a small share of requests, so I’d check p99 and pause logs, not the average.”

takeaways: Reachable from roots means alive; cycles are collected.
Time between collections is headroom divided by allocation rate.
Pauses hurt the tail, not the average.
Keep the heap limit below the container limit.

interactive.title: Spend memory or CPU?
interactive.prompt: Live data is 1.5 GB in a 2 GB heap and the service allocates 1.2 GB/s. You can raise the heap to 4 GB. How does the number of collections change?

choices.label: About 5 times fewer collections
choices.feedback: Right: headroom grows from 0.5 GB to 2.5 GB, so the interval grows fivefold.

choices.label: About 2 times fewer, matching the heap
choices.feedback: The heap doubles, but only the space above live data buys time, and that grows fivefold.

choices.label: About the same, since live data has not changed
choices.feedback: Live data sets the cost of each collection, not how often they happen.

interactive.reveal: Interval = (heap − live) ÷ allocation rate: 0.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.42 s before and 2.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 2.1 s after. Each collection traces the same 1.5 GB, so total collector CPU falls by about the same factor.

title: CPU Caches, Locality and False Sharing
objectives: Explain why memory access patterns can change speed tenfold or more
Estimate the cost of cache misses from rough latencies
Spot and fix false sharing between threads

cards.title: Memory moves in 64-byte lines
cards.body: The CPU never reads a single byte from main memory; it fetches a whole cache line, 64 bytes on most current processors, into a hierarchy of caches. A hit in the smallest cache takes around a nanosecond, while a trip to main memory takes on the order of 100 ns (rough figures that vary by machine). Programs are fast when the next data they need is already in a line they fetched, and slow when each access lands somewhere new.

cards.title: Worked example: an array against a linked list
cards.body: Same 10 million values, same sum, very different memory traffic.
steps: 10 million 4-byte integers in an array occupy 40 MB in consecutive lines
The hardware prefetcher sees the sequential pattern and streams lines ahead: at about 10 GB/s the sum takes about 4 ms
The same values in a linked list whose nodes are scattered across the heap cost roughly one cache miss per node
10,000,000 misses × about 80 ns ≈ 0.8 s, around 200 times slower for the same arithmetic
Lesson: contiguous layouts and predictable access often matter more than the operation count (all latencies illustrative)

cards.title: Keeping lines coherent across cores
cards.body: Each core has its own small caches, so when one core writes a line, copies held by other cores must be invalidated before the write completes. The hardware does this automatically, which keeps memory consistent, but every write to a line another core is using turns into traffic between cores. Data written by one thread and read by many is cheap only if writes are rare.

cards.title: Trap: false sharing between per-thread counters
cards.body: Eight threads each increment their own counter, and the counters sit next to each other in an array. There is no shared variable in the code, yet the program scales worse than a single thread, because all eight counters share one 64-byte line and every increment steals that line from the other cores. Pad or align each hot per-thread value to its own line, or keep it in a local variable and combine at the end.

cards.title: Misconception: fewer instructions always run faster
cards.body: An algorithm that does fewer operations but jumps around memory can lose to one that does more work on contiguous data. Binary search over a sorted array of a few thousand keys often beats a tree with the same keys, and scanning a small array can beat a hash lookup. Compare candidates by memory accesses and measure on realistic sizes before trusting the operation count.

questions.prompt: A loop reads one byte, skips 63, reads the next byte, and so on through a large buffer. Compared with reading every byte, roughly how much memory traffic does it cause?

choices.label: One sixty-fourth of the traffic, matching the bytes it reads
Half the traffic, because the prefetcher skips alternate lines
About the same traffic, since each read pulls a full line
Twice the traffic, because each skipped line is fetched twice

questions.explanation: Memory moves in 64-byte lines, so touching one byte per line still fetches every line: the bytes skipped were transferred anyway. Traffic would drop to a sixty-fourth only if bytes moved individually, prefetchers fetch more lines rather than fewer, and nothing fetches a line twice in a single forward pass.

questions.prompt: Eight threads each increment a separate counter in an array of eight 8-byte longs. Throughput drops as threads are added. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The counters share one cache line, so cores keep stealing it
Separate counters need a lock, and the threads wait on it
Eight threads exceed what the scheduler can run on eight cores
Integer increments are slow when several cores run them together

questions.explanation: Eight 8-byte counters fill exactly one 64-byte line, so each write invalidates the line in seven other caches. No lock is involved because the variables are distinct, eight threads on eight cores is a normal fit, and an increment on a line the core already owns is fast.

questions.prompt: A two-dimensional grid is stored row by row. A loop sums it column by column, with the column as its outer loop. What usually speeds it up the most?

choices.label: Using a smaller integer type for the loop counters
Running the column loop on several threads
Swapping the loops so the row index changes slowest
Storing the grid as one row array per thread instead

questions.explanation: Walking a row-major grid column by column jumps a full row between accesses, so nearly every read is a new line. Swapping the loops makes accesses sequential and lets the prefetcher stream lines. Counter types barely matter, threads multiply the same miss pattern, and per-thread row arrays do not fix the access order.

questions.prompt: A configuration object is read by every request on 32 cores and rewritten once a minute. A hit counter beside it is written by every request. Which change helps the most?

choices.label: Copy the configuration into each thread on every request
Make the configuration read-only and reload it in place
Put a lock around reads of the configuration object
Move the hit counter to its own line or make it per-core

questions.explanation: Reads of a line that nobody writes are cheap on every core; the problem is the counter, whose constant writes invalidate the line holding the configuration too. Copying on every request adds work, the configuration is already effectively read-only, and a lock adds a contended write on every read.

questions.prompt: A lookup does 5 million random accesses into a 4 GB table, and each one misses every cache and costs about 100 ns. Roughly how many milliseconds do the accesses take?
assumptions: Accesses do not overlap
Each access costs a full memory round trip
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same 5 million accesses hitting the first-level cache at about 1 ns would take about 5 ms, so layout and locality can matter a hundredfold. Real CPUs overlap some independent misses, so measure before relying on the exact figure.

questions.prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest typical access latency.

items.label: Main memory
First-level cache
Local SSD read
Last-level (shared) cache

questions.explanation: Roughly 1 ns, tens of nanoseconds, about 100 ns, then tens to hundreds of microseconds for a solid-state disk.

flashcards.back: 64 bytes on most current CPUs; memory always moves a line at a time.
Threads write different variables on the same line, so cores keep invalidating each other.
Pad or align hot per-thread data to separate lines, or accumulate locally and combine.
