mechanism.title: What happens on a memory access
steps: The CPU translates the virtual address, then checks its first-level data cache, typically tens of kilobytes per core with a latency of a few cycles.
On a miss it checks the second-level cache (per core, hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes) and then the shared last-level cache (several to tens of megabytes), each larger and slower.

If every cache misses, the request goes to main memory, costing on the order of 100 ns, enough time for hundreds of simple instructions. The whole 64-byte line containing the address comes back and is placed in the caches.

Prefetchers watch access patterns. Sequential or constant-stride access is detected and future lines are requested before they are needed, which is why scanning an array runs near memory bandwidth rather than at miss latency.

When a core writes a line, the coherence protocol invalidates copies in other cores. A later read by another core must fetch the line from the writer, which costs tens of nanoseconds and serialises cores that write the same line.

Dependent loads (following a pointer to get the next address) cannot be overlapped, so a pointer-chasing structure pays the full miss latency at each step, while independent loads in an array can be in flight together.

useWhen: Use contiguous arrays and structure layouts that match the access order of hot loops.
Use per-thread or per-core accumulators, padded to a line, for counters written on every operation.
avoidWhen: Avoid pointer-heavy structures in hot paths over large data sets.
Avoid placing frequently written fields next to fields that many threads read.

rows: Random access into a large table
Batch, sort or partition by key
Use arrays or allocate nodes together

numbers.title: What false sharing costs a counter loop
assumptions: Each thread does 100 million increments (illustrative)
About 1 ns per increment on a line the core owns; about 50 ns when the line must be fetched from another core (illustrative orders of magnitude)
steps: Padded counters: 100,000,000 × 1 ns = 0.1 s per thread, all threads in parallel.
Shared line, worst case: each increment pays about 50 ns, so 100,000,000 × 50 ns = 5 s per thread.
The 8-thread run takes about 5 s instead of 0.1 s, slower than one thread doing all 800 million increments alone (0.8 s).
Padding each counter to 64 bytes uses 8 × 64 = 512 bytes instead of 64, a negligible cost.
numbers.result: False sharing can make a parallel loop about 50 times slower than its padded version and slower than running it on one thread; 448 extra bytes of padding remove it.

india.title: Finding false sharing with a profiler
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s Visual Studio documentation describes false sharing as threads updating different variables that sit on the same cache line, which forces the line to bounce between cores even though no data is actually shared. Its profiler can flag the hot field and the competing threads; the usual fix it shows is padding or reorganising the structure so each thread’s frequently written data occupies a separate cache line.

pitfalls.trap: “Each thread has its own variable, so there’s no contention.”
pitfalls.say: “Distinct variables can still share a 64-byte line; I’d check layout and pad hot per-thread fields.”

pitfalls.trap: “The tree does fewer comparisons, so it must be faster.”
pitfalls.say: “For small data the array may win on cache misses; I’d benchmark both at real sizes.”

takeaways: Memory moves in 64-byte lines.
A miss to main memory costs around 100 ns, roughly a hundred times a first-level hit.
Contiguous, predictable access lets prefetching hide latency.
Writes to a shared line serialise cores, even for distinct variables.

interactive.title: Why does adding threads slow it down?
interactive.prompt: Four threads each count matching records in their quarter of an array, storing the running count in results[threadIndex], an array of four 8-byte integers. One thread takes 2 s; four threads take 3 s.

choices.label: The four counts share a cache line, so every increment bounces it between cores
choices.feedback: Right: four 8-byte slots fit in one 64-byte line, and each write invalidates the other three caches.

choices.label: The array of records is too large to split across four threads
choices.feedback: Each thread reads its own contiguous quarter, which is the ideal parallel pattern.

choices.label: The threads need a lock around results, and they are waiting on it
choices.feedback: Each thread writes only its own slot, so no lock is needed or used.

interactive.reveal: Count in a local variable inside each thread and write results[threadIndex] once at the end, or pad each slot to 64 bytes. Either makes the four threads independent, and the run should approach 0.5 s.

seeAlso.why: Virtual memory and the TLB sit just in front of the caches
Atomics and contended counters pay the same line-transfer cost
Moving a thread to another core leaves its warm cache behind

title: Atomics, Compare-and-Swap and Memory Ordering
objectives: Use atomic operations and compare-and-swap loops correctly
Explain why compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations, and how acquire and release prevent it
Recognise the ABA problem and contention limits of lock-free code

cards.title: One indivisible step
cards.body: An atomic operation reads and updates a memory location so that no other thread can see it half done. Atomic increments, exchanges and compare-and-swap (CAS) are single hardware instructions on common CPUs. CAS takes an address, an expected value and a new value: it writes the new value only if the location still holds the expected one, and reports whether it succeeded. Almost every lock-free structure is built from it.

cards.title: Worked example: a CAS retry loop
cards.body: Updating a shared maximum without a lock.
steps: Read the current maximum: 40
Compute the new value locally: this thread saw 57, so the new maximum is 57
CAS(max, expected 40, new 57); meanwhile another thread already stored 52, so the CAS fails and returns 52
Recompute with the fresh value: 57 is still larger, so try CAS(max, 52, 57), which succeeds
If the fresh value had been 60, the loop would stop without writing: never overwrite a newer value blindly

cards.title: Why a plain flag is not enough
cards.body: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations when a single thread cannot tell the difference, so another thread can see a ready flag set before the data it guards. A release store on the flag guarantees that earlier writes become visible first; an acquire load on the flag guarantees that later reads see them. Paired together they publish data safely, which is what a mutex does for you on lock and unlock.

cards.title: Trap: the ABA problem
cards.body: A lock-free stack pops by reading the top node A and its next pointer, then CASing the top from A to next. If, in between, another thread pops A, pops B, and pushes A back, the CAS still sees A and succeeds, installing a pointer to B, which was freed. Equal values do not mean nothing changed. Counters (tagged pointers) or deferred freeing schemes such as hazard pointers or epochs prevent it.

cards.title: Misconception: lock-free means fast under contention
cards.body: Every successful atomic write needs exclusive ownership of its cache line, so 32 cores hammering one atomic counter queue up for that line just as they would for a lock, and failed CAS attempts waste work on top. Lock-free code guarantees that some thread always makes progress; it does not make a contended location scale. Shard hot counters per core and sum them when read.

questions.prompt: A thread increments a shared counter with a CAS loop: read v, compute v + 1, CAS(counter, v, v + 1). What must happen when the CAS fails?

choices.label: Write v + 1 with a plain store, since the CAS already checked
Give up, because another thread has done the increment
Wait for the other thread to finish, then retry the same CAS
Read the current value again, recompute, and retry the CAS

questions.explanation: A failure means another thread changed the counter after this thread read it, so the computed value is stale and must be recomputed from the fresh one. A plain store would overwrite the other update, giving up loses this increment, and retrying with the old expected value can never succeed.

questions.prompt: A producer writes a record and then sets ready = true with ordinary, non-atomic writes. A consumer on another core loops until ready is true and reads the record. Which outcome is possible?

choices.label: The consumer sees ready but reads an old or partial record
Nothing bad: writes always become visible in program order
The record is safe, but ready may flip back to false later
The consumer reads the record twice and double counts it

questions.explanation: Without release and acquire ordering, the compiler or CPU may make the flag visible before the record, so the consumer can read stale data. Program order is not guaranteed across cores. Nothing writes false again, so the flag cannot flip back, and the consumer reads the record once; the danger is reading it too early.

questions.prompt: A lock-free stack uses CAS on the top pointer. Under heavy load it sometimes returns a node that was already freed. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: CAS is not atomic on the machine’s pointer size
The top changed from A and back to A between the read and CAS
Two threads pushed at once and both CAS operations succeeded
The stack grew larger than the CPU cache could hold

questions.explanation: That is the ABA problem: the CAS compares only the pointer value, so a node that was popped and pushed back looks unchanged while its next pointer is stale. Pointer-width CAS is atomic on mainstream CPUs, two CAS operations on the same expected value cannot both succeed, and cache size affects speed, not correctness.

questions.prompt: A request counter is a single atomic integer incremented by every request on 64 cores. Profiling shows time spent on that increment. What is the best fix?

choices.label: Replace the atomic with a mutex around a plain integer
Use a CAS loop instead of an atomic add instruction
Keep a counter per core and sum them when read
Mark the counter volatile so it skips the CPU cache

questions.explanation: The cost is 64 cores taking turns owning one cache line. Per-core counters keep each line local, and the rare reader adds them up. A mutex has the same single hot line plus waiting, a CAS loop adds failed retries, and volatile does not bypass the cache or make increments atomic.

questions.prompt: Under contention each CAS attempt succeeds with probability 0.25, independently. On average, how many attempts does one update take?
assumptions: Attempts succeed or fail independently
The success chance stays at 0.25
questions.explanation: Design implication: wasted attempts grow as the success rate falls, so at 5% success each update takes 20 tries; reducing sharing helps far more than tuning the loop.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of safely publishing a record from one thread to another.

items.label: Producer sets the ready flag with a release store
Consumer reads the record’s fields
Producer writes every field of the record
Consumer reads the ready flag with an acquire load and sees true

questions.explanation: Release after the writes, acquire before the reads: everything written before the release is visible after the matching acquire.

flashcards.back: Write new only if the location still holds expected; report success. Retry with a fresh read on failure.
Release store publishes earlier writes; an acquire load that sees it makes them visible to later reads.
A value changes and changes back, so CAS succeeds on stale assumptions; use tags or deferred freeing.

mechanism.title: What an atomic operation does in hardware
steps: To perform an atomic read-modify-write, the core must own the cache line exclusively. If another core holds a copy, the coherence protocol invalidates it first, which takes tens of nanoseconds when the line is elsewhere.
While the core owns the line, it performs the read and the write without letting any other core access the line in between, so the operation appears indivisible to every thread.
Compare-and-swap returns whether the location held the expected value. Software builds loops on top: read, compute, CAS, and on failure use the value just returned to recompute.

Separately, compilers reorder and cache values in registers, and CPUs let loads overtake stores and buffer writes. Single-threaded results stay the same, but other cores may observe operations in a different order.

Ordering constraints (release, acquire, or full barriers) limit that reordering. A release store keeps earlier memory operations before it; an acquire load keeps later operations after it. Locks include both, which is why code using a mutex correctly needs no explicit barriers.

Lock-free structures must also reclaim memory safely: a node removed by one thread may still be read by another. Schemes such as hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation delay freeing until no thread can hold a reference, which also prevents ABA on reused nodes.

useWhen: Use atomics for counters, flags and single-word state shared between threads.
Use CAS loops when an update depends on the current value and must not lose concurrent changes.
avoidWhen: Avoid hand-written lock-free structures where a mutex or a tested library structure would do.
Avoid relying on ordinary variables for signalling between threads.

rows: Exclusion plus ordering for a whole section

numbers.title: When a shared counter stops scaling
assumptions: Each atomic increment on a contended line costs about 50 ns while the line moves between cores (illustrative)
Per-core counters cost about 1 ns per increment (illustrative)
steps: One contended line serves increments one at a time: 1 ÷ 50 ns = 20 million increments a second in total, however many cores try.
A service doing 50 million increments a second cannot be served by that line at all.
With per-core counters each core handles its own: 64 cores × (1 ÷ 1 ns) leaves the counter far from any limit.
Reading the total sums 64 values, about 64 cache misses, which is fine for a metrics scrape every few seconds.
numbers.result: A single contended atomic caps the whole machine at roughly 20 million updates a second in this example; sharding by core removes the cap at the cost of a slower, rare read.

india.title: How the Linux kernel documents memory ordering
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s memory-barriers document explains that CPUs and compilers may reorder memory accesses, and that without barriers one CPU can observe another’s stores in a different order than they were issued. It describes acquire and release operations as one-way barriers and shows the classic message-passing pattern: write the data, then publish a flag with release semantics, and read the flag with acquire semantics before reading the data.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s atomic, so it’s thread-safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Each atomic is safe alone; invariants across several fields still need a lock or careful ordering.”

pitfalls.trap: “Lock-free will fix the contention.”
pitfalls.say: “A single hot line still serialises cores; I’d shard the counter per core first.”

takeaways: CAS writes only if the value is unchanged; on failure, re-read and recompute.
Use release to publish and acquire to read published data.
Equal values do not prove nothing changed: beware ABA.
A hot atomic serialises cores; shard it.

interactive.title: Is this flag safe?
interactive.prompt: Thread A fills a buffer and then sets done = true as an atomic store with relaxed ordering. Thread B loops until an atomic relaxed load of done returns true, then reads the buffer.

choices.label: Unsafe: relaxed ordering lets B see done before the buffer
choices.feedback: Right: relaxed atomics only make the flag itself indivisible; they do not order the buffer writes.

choices.label: Safe: any atomic flag orders the memory around it
choices.feedback: Only acquire, release or stronger orderings constrain surrounding accesses.

choices.label: Safe on every CPU because stores are never reordered
choices.feedback: Compilers can reorder too, and some CPUs reorder stores freely.

interactive.reveal: Make the store a release and the load an acquire. Then everything A wrote before setting done is guaranteed visible to B once B sees done = true, on every CPU and compiler.

seeAlso.why: Mutexes give you atomicity and ordering in one tool
Atomics pay the cache-line transfer cost described there
Lock-free code avoids deadlock but brings its own failure modes

title: cgroups: CPU Throttling and Memory Limits
objectives: Explain how a CPU quota is enforced per period and why it causes latency spikes
Distinguish CPU weights from CPU limits, and memory.high from memory.max
Predict what counts against a container’s memory limit

cards.title: What a container limit really is
cards.body: A container is ordinary processes placed in a control group (cgroup), a kernel object that accounts for and limits resources for every process inside it. CPU can be shared by weight, which only matters when CPUs are busy, or capped by a quota: a number of CPU-microseconds the group may use in each period, 100 ms by default. Memory has a soft throttle point (memory.high) and a hard limit (memory.max).

cards.title: Worked example: a 2-CPU limit with 16 busy threads
cards.body: Quota is spent in wall-clock time across all threads at once.
steps: Limit: 2 CPUs, which is 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period
16 threads become runnable together at the start of a period on a 32-core machine
They burn 16 CPU-ms per millisecond, so the 200 ms quota is gone after 200 ÷ 16 = 12.5 ms
Every thread in the group is then throttled for the remaining 87.5 ms of the period
A request needing 13 ms of work now takes over 100 ms, although average CPU use looks far below the limit

cards.title: Requests, weights and limits are different knobs
cards.body: A CPU weight (what an orchestrator’s CPU request usually sets) decides how contended CPU is divided and never stops a group from using idle cores. A CPU quota (what a CPU limit sets) is a hard cap enforced even when the machine is idle. Many teams set requests for fair placement and leave CPU limits off or generous for latency-sensitive services, because throttling hurts tail latency even when there is spare capacity.

cards.title: Trap: files in a memory-backed directory count as memory
cards.body: Writing a large file into a tmpfs directory (such as an in-memory scratch volume or /dev/shm) uses memory charged to the container. So do page cache pages for files the container reads and writes, though clean cache can be reclaimed. A job that writes 3 GB of temporary files to a memory-backed volume inside a 4 GB limit can be killed while its own heap is small. Put large scratch data on disk-backed storage.

cards.title: Misconception: the memory limit is enforced like a heap limit
cards.body: At memory.high the kernel throttles the group and reclaims its memory aggressively, so the process slows down rather than failing. At memory.max, if reclaim cannot free enough, the kernel’s OOM killer terminates a process in the group with SIGKILL. The program gets no allocation error and cannot clean up; it simply disappears, and the orchestrator reports it as killed for out-of-memory.

questions.prompt: A service with a 1-CPU limit averages 40% CPU, yet its p99 latency jumps to over 100 ms every few seconds. What should you check first?

choices.label: Whether its throttled time counters are rising
Whether the node has fewer physical cores than containers
Whether its memory limit is lower than its CPU limit
Whether the load average on the node is above one

questions.explanation: Averages hide bursts: a burst of parallel threads can spend a whole period’s quota in a few milliseconds and then wait for the next period, which the cgroup reports in its throttling counters. Packing more containers than cores is normal with weights, memory and CPU limits are not compared, and node load average reflects every container, not this group’s quota.

questions.prompt: A container has a CPU request of 1 and no CPU limit on an otherwise idle 8-core node. How much CPU can it use?

choices.label: Exactly one CPU, because the request is enforced as a cap
Up to all 8 cores while nothing else wants them
Half a CPU until the scheduler measures its real usage
None until another container on the node is also running

questions.explanation: A request becomes a weight that only divides contended CPU, so on an idle node the container can use every core. It is a limit, not a request, that sets a hard quota. Nothing starts at half a CPU or waits for a neighbour to run.

questions.prompt: A worker with a 2 GB memory limit and a 400 MB heap is killed for out-of-memory while extracting a 1.8 GB archive into an in-memory scratch volume. Why?

choices.label: The heap grew briefly to 2 GB while reading the archive
The archive’s compressed bytes were counted twice by the kernel
Files in the memory-backed volume count against the limit
Extraction raised the CPU usage, which lowered the memory cap

questions.explanation: tmpfs pages are memory, charged to the container, so 1.8 GB of files plus a 400 MB heap exceeds 2 GB. Nothing suggests a heap spike, compressed input is not double counted, and CPU usage never changes the memory limit.

questions.prompt: What happens when a container’s memory usage reaches memory.max and the kernel cannot reclaim enough?

choices.label: The next allocation returns an error the program can handle
The container is paused until memory is freed elsewhere
Its pages are moved to the node’s other containers
A process in the group is killed with SIGKILL

questions.explanation: The cgroup OOM killer picks a process in the group and sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, so there is no cleanup and the exit code is 137. Allocations typically succeed until the pages are touched, so there is no handleable error; there is no pausing, and memory is never moved to other containers.

questions.prompt: A container’s quota is 100 ms of CPU per 100 ms period (1 CPU). Eight threads start running together on a large machine. After how many milliseconds is the quota used up?
assumptions: All 8 threads run in parallel on separate cores
The period starts when they start
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the group is then throttled for 87.5 ms of every 100 ms period, which is why a parallel burst in a small container shows long stalls even though the average CPU use is only one core.

questions.prompt: Order what happens as a container’s memory use keeps growing toward its limits.

items.label: Usage reaches memory.max and reclaim cannot free enough
Usage passes memory.high and the group is throttled under heavy reclaim
The OOM killer sends SIGKILL to a process in the group
The kernel reclaims clean page cache and swaps if allowed

questions.explanation: Throttle and reclaim first, then the hard limit, then the kill; memory.high slows a group down, only memory.max kills.

flashcards.back: CPU time allowed per period (default period 100 ms); when spent, the whole group waits for the next period.
Request: weight for contended CPU and placement. Limit: hard quota, enforced even on an idle node.
high: throttle and reclaim, no kill. max: hard limit; the OOM killer sends SIGKILL.

sources.title: Control Group v2, Linux kernel documentation
Resource Management for Pods and Containers, Kubernetes

mechanism.title: How the kernel enforces CPU and memory limits
steps: Every process belongs to one cgroup in a hierarchy. Controllers enabled for that group (cpu, memory, io, pids) charge the group for what its processes use and apply its limits.

For CPU, the cpu.weight file sets a relative share used only when CPUs are contended. The cpu.max file holds a quota and a period, such as 200000 100000, meaning 200 ms of CPU per 100 ms: two CPUs’ worth.

The scheduler deducts run time from the group’s quota as any of its threads run on any core. When the quota hits zero, all the group’s threads are taken off the CPU until the next period refills it. The cpu.stat file counts how many periods were throttled and the total throttled time.
For memory, every page the group’s processes allocate, including page cache for files they touch, tmpfs files and kernel memory such as socket buffers, is charged to the group.

Above memory.high the kernel throttles allocations and reclaims aggressively; this never invokes the OOM killer. Reaching memory.max forces reclaim, and if that fails, the OOM killer picks a process within the group and kills it.

Runtimes that size thread pools or heaps from the machine instead of the cgroup will oversubscribe: 64 threads under a 2-CPU quota burn the quota quickly, and a heap sized for 64 GB will be killed at a 4 GB limit.

useWhen: Use CPU requests (weights) for every container so the scheduler places and shares fairly.
Use memory limits everywhere, with heap and buffer settings sized below them.
avoidWhen: Avoid tight CPU limits on latency-sensitive services with bursty parallel work.
Avoid large scratch files on memory-backed volumes inside a small memory limit.

columns: Effect when the node is idle
rows: SIGKILL from the OOM killer, exit 137

numbers.title: How a CPU limit stretches one burst
assumptions: A request fans out to 20 threads, each needing 15 ms of CPU, on a machine with plenty of idle cores (illustrative)
The container’s limit is 2 CPUs: 200 ms per 100 ms period
steps: Total CPU needed: 20 × 15 ms = 300 ms.
Period 1: 20 threads use 20 CPU-ms per ms, so the 200 ms quota is gone at 10 ms; each thread has done 10 ms and needs 5 ms more.
Throttled until the period ends at 100 ms; period 2 refills 200 ms and the remaining 100 ms of work takes 5 ms.
The request finishes at about 105 ms. Without the limit it would finish at 15 ms; with a 3-CPU limit (300 ms quota) it would finish within the first period, at 15 ms.
numbers.result: A CPU limit that is ample on average turned a 15 ms burst into a 105 ms response, seven times slower; size limits for peak parallelism or rely on requests alone.

india.title: How the kernel documents memory.high
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s cgroup v2 documentation describes memory.high as a throttle limit: when a group’s usage goes over it, the group’s processes are throttled and put under heavy reclaim pressure, and going over the high limit never invokes the OOM killer. It describes memory.max as the hard limit, where the OOM killer is invoked if usage cannot be reduced. Kubernetes’ resource documentation adds that CPU limits are enforced by throttling, while a container exceeding its memory limit may be killed.

pitfalls.trap: “CPU averages 40% of the limit, so the limit isn’t a problem.”
pitfalls.say: “Quotas are enforced per 100 ms period; I’d check throttled periods in cpu.stat.”

pitfalls.trap: “It was OOM killed, so the heap leaked.”
pitfalls.say: “The cgroup counts page cache, tmpfs and native memory too; I’d break down memory.stat first.”

takeaways: A CPU limit is a quota per 100 ms period, spent across all threads at once.
Parallel bursts get throttled even when average use is low.
Requests set weights; limits set hard caps.
memory.max kills with SIGKILL; tmpfs and page cache count too.

interactive.title: How long does the burst take?
interactive.prompt: A container limited to 2 CPUs (200 ms per 100 ms period) gets a request that fans out to 20 threads of 15 ms CPU work each. The node has 32 idle cores.

choices.label: About 105 ms, because the quota runs out at 10 ms and the rest waits for the next period
choices.feedback: Right: 200 ms of quota covers 10 ms on 20 threads; the last 5 ms each runs after the refill at 100 ms.

choices.label: About 15 ms, because 32 idle cores can run all 20 threads
choices.feedback: Idle cores do not help once the group’s quota is spent.

choices.label: About 150 ms, because 300 ms of work at 2 CPUs takes 150 ms
choices.feedback: That assumes smooth use of two CPUs; quota is spent in parallel bursts and refilled only at period boundaries.

interactive.reveal: Throttling is all-or-nothing per period, so the finish time is set by period boundaries, not by average CPU. Fewer threads, a higher limit or no limit would all finish within the first period.

seeAlso.why: The scheduler that enforces quotas and weights
Orchestrators set these cgroup values from requests and limits
An OOM kill arrives as SIGKILL with exit code 137

title: File Descriptors and Resource Limits
objectives: Explain what a file descriptor is and what consumes one
Size a process’s descriptor limit from its connections and files
Diagnose “too many open files” and descriptor leaks

cards.title: A small integer for every open thing
cards.body: A file descriptor is an index into a process’s table of open kernel objects: files, sockets, pipes, event queues, timers. Every open, accept, socket, pipe or epoll call returns the lowest free number, and close frees it. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold (RLIMIT_NOFILE, commonly 1,024 by default for the soft limit on many Linux systems), and the whole system has a global limit too.

cards.title: Worked example: how many clients fit under the limit?
cards.body: A proxy uses two descriptors per client: one inbound, one to the backend.
steps: Soft limit: 1,024 descriptors
Already used: 24 for standard streams, log files, listening sockets and the event queue
Clients that fit: (1,024 − 24) ÷ 2 = 500
Raising the soft limit to 65,536 gives (65,536 − 24) ÷ 2 = 32,756 clients
Client 501 fails at accept with EMFILE: a per-process error, not a sign that the machine is out of memory

cards.title: Trap: a descriptor leak looks like a capacity problem
cards.body: A code path that opens a file or connection and returns early on an error without closing it leaks one descriptor each time. Nothing fails for days; then accept and open start returning EMFILE and the service stops taking traffic, and a restart “fixes” it. Watch the count of open descriptors per process, release them in a finally or scoped block, and treat a count that climbs steadily under flat traffic as a leak.

cards.title: Misconception: an EMFILE error goes away on its own
cards.body: An event loop that hits EMFILE on accept leaves the pending connection in the listen queue. With level-triggered readiness, the listening socket stays readable, so the loop wakes immediately, fails accept again, and spins at full CPU while doing nothing useful. Back off or temporarily stop watching the listening socket, and some servers keep one spare descriptor to accept and immediately close the excess connection.

cards.title: Descriptors survive fork and exec unless told not to
cards.body: A child created by fork gets copies of all the parent’s descriptors, and they stay open across exec unless marked close-on-exec. A helper program launched by a server can then hold the server’s listening socket or database connections, so the port stays busy after the server exits and connections never close. Open descriptors with the close-on-exec flag by default.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT use up a file descriptor in the process that calls it?

choices.label: Accepting a new TCP connection
Creating a pipe to a child process
Allocating a 1 MB buffer on the heap
Creating an epoll instance to watch sockets

questions.explanation: Heap memory is managed by the allocator and never appears in the descriptor table. Accept returns a new socket descriptor, a pipe returns two descriptors (one for each end), and an epoll instance is itself a descriptor.

questions.prompt: A proxy starts failing new connections with “Too many open files” at about 500 clients. Memory and CPU are fine. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The kernel ran out of memory for socket buffers
The soft descriptor limit of 1,024 is used at two per client
The listen backlog is full, so the kernel resets new clients
The system-wide file table limit for all users was reached

questions.explanation: Two descriptors per proxied client reach a 1,024 soft limit at about 500 clients, and the error name says so. Socket buffer exhaustion shows different errors, a full backlog drops or resets connections without “too many open files”, and the system-wide table gives ENFILE (“too many open files in system”), not the per-process EMFILE.

questions.prompt: Open descriptors for a service rise by about 300 an hour under steady traffic and drop to normal after each restart. Which code is the most likely culprit?

choices.label: An error path that returns before closing a file it opened
A cache that holds parsed objects in memory without a limit
A thread pool that keeps its idle worker threads alive
A logger that writes every request to one open file

questions.explanation: A leak grows with the number of times the faulty path runs and resets on restart. An unbounded cache leaks memory, not descriptors; idle threads hold no descriptors of their own; and a logger writing to one open file uses one descriptor for its whole life.

questions.prompt: After accept fails with EMFILE, an event-loop server pins a core at 100% CPU and serves nothing. Why?

choices.label: The kernel retries the failed accept in a busy loop
The rejected client keeps retrying faster and faster
The listener stays readable, so the loop wakes and fails again
The error disables the event queue and falls back to polling

questions.explanation: The pending connection is still queued, so a level-triggered event loop is told again and again that the listener is ready, and each accept fails at once. The kernel does not retry for you, the client is just waiting in the queue, and EMFILE does not disable the event queue.

questions.prompt: A proxy has a limit of 4,096 descriptors, uses 40 for itself, and needs 2 per client. How many clients can it serve at once?
assumptions: Every client holds both descriptors for the whole session
No other files are opened per request
questions.explanation: Sanity check: forgetting the backend connection doubles the estimate to about 4,056, so count every descriptor a request holds (upstream connections, temporary files) and leave headroom for bursts.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to confirm and fix a suspected descriptor leak.

items.label: Compare the growth with traffic to see if it climbs under flat load
Find the code path that opens that kind and add a guaranteed close
Track open descriptor counts for the process over time
List what the open descriptors point to and find the dominant kind

questions.explanation: Measure, correlate with load, classify what is leaking, then fix the path that opens it.

flashcards.back: A per-process integer naming an open kernel object: file, socket, pipe, event queue.
EMFILE: this process hit its limit. ENFILE: the whole system’s file table is full.
A flag that closes a descriptor when the process execs, so children don’t inherit sockets or files.

mechanism.title: What happens when a process opens something
steps: The process calls open, socket, accept, pipe or a similar call. The kernel creates or finds the kernel object (an open file description holding the offset and flags, or a socket).

The kernel then picks the lowest unused number in the process’s descriptor table and points that slot at the object. If the table already holds as many entries as the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE allows, the call fails with EMFILE.

Separately, the system tracks the total number of open files across all processes; when that global limit is reached, calls fail with ENFILE, which points at the whole machine rather than one process.

Duplicating a descriptor (dup, or fork copying the table) makes two numbers point at one open file description, which shares the file offset. The object is released only when the last descriptor referring to it is closed.
At exec, descriptors marked close-on-exec are closed and the rest stay open in the new program. Libraries that open descriptors without the flag leak them into every child process.
The soft limit can be raised by the process up to the hard limit; only a privileged process can raise the hard limit. Service managers and container runtimes set both when they start the process.

useWhen: Raise the soft limit for servers that hold many connections, and size it from clients × descriptors per client.
Open descriptors with close-on-exec unless a child must inherit them.
avoidWhen: Avoid raising limits to hide a leak; the count will reach any limit eventually.
Avoid a tight accept retry loop after EMFILE.

rows: Raise the soft limit or fix the leak
Find the process holding the most
Child kept the listener without close-on-exec
Close in finally or a scoped block

numbers.title: Sizing the limit for a connection-heavy service
assumptions: Target: 20,000 concurrent clients through a proxy (illustrative)
Per client: 1 inbound socket and 1 upstream socket; 50 fixed descriptors; 25% headroom for bursts and slow closes
steps: Descriptors for clients: 20,000 × 2 = 40,000.
Add fixed descriptors: 40,000 + 50 = 40,050.
Round up to the next common setting: 65,536, which also leaves room for sockets lingering after close.
numbers.result: A 20,000-client proxy needs a descriptor limit around 50,000; the 1,024 default would cap it at about 500 clients.

india.title: What the manual says about running out
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The accept(2) manual page lists two distinct errors: EMFILE when the per-process limit on the number of open file descriptors has been reached, and ENFILE when the system-wide limit on the total number of open files has been reached. The getrlimit(2) page describes RLIMIT_NOFILE as one greater than the maximum descriptor number the process may open, and explains that an unprivileged process may raise its soft limit only up to its hard limit.

pitfalls.trap: “We get ‘too many open files’, so the disk is full.”
pitfalls.say: “It means the descriptor limit; I’d count open descriptors and check if they grow under flat load.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just set the limit to a million.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d size it from clients × descriptors each, and fix any leak first.”

takeaways: Every file, socket, pipe and event queue uses a descriptor.
EMFILE is per process; ENFILE is system-wide.
A steady climb under flat traffic is a leak.
Use close-on-exec so children don’t inherit descriptors.

interactive.title: What happens at client 501?
interactive.prompt: A proxy runs with the default soft limit of 1,024 descriptors, uses 24 of its own, and opens one inbound and one upstream socket per client. Clients keep arriving.

choices.label: Accept fails with EMFILE once about 500 clients are connected
choices.feedback: Right: (1,024 − 24) ÷ 2 = 500 clients use every remaining descriptor.

choices.label: The kernel raises the limit automatically when it is reached
choices.feedback: Limits never grow by themselves; the process or its service manager must raise the soft limit.

choices.label: New clients succeed but the oldest connections are closed
choices.feedback: The kernel never closes existing descriptors to make room.

interactive.reveal: Size the limit from clients × descriptors per client plus headroom. Also make the event loop handle EMFILE without spinning, by backing off or pausing the listener until descriptors are free.

seeAlso.why: Every descriptor is created and used through system calls
Event loops watch descriptors for readiness
Pooled connections each hold a descriptor for their whole life

title: Amdahl’s Law: How Far More Cores Go
objectives: Compute the speedup limit set by the serial part of a job
Explain why contention can make extra cores slow a job down
Decide between more cores, less serial work, or a bigger problem size

cards.title: The serial part sets the ceiling
cards.body: If a fraction p of a job’s work can run in parallel and the rest must run one step at a time, then on N cores the speedup is 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ N). As N grows the parallel term shrinks toward zero, so the speedup can never exceed 1 ÷ (1 − p). With 95% parallel work the ceiling is 20 times, whether you have 64 cores or 6,400.

cards.title: Worked example: 95% parallel, more and more cores
cards.body: Each doubling of cores buys less than the one before.
steps: 1,000 cores: 1 ÷ (0.05 + 0.00095) ≈ 19.6 times, almost at the ceiling of 20
Going from 8 to 32 cores quadruples the hardware for about 2.1 times the speed
Cost per job (cores × time) rises by about 1.9 times, so the extra speed is paid for in efficiency

cards.title: Trap: contention makes the curve bend back down
cards.body: Amdahl’s law assumes the serial part stays fixed. Real systems also pay for coordination: a lock, a shared counter or a cache line that every core touches costs more as cores are added, because they queue for it. Past some point throughput falls as cores increase. If adding cores makes a job slower, look for a shared hot spot before buying hardware.

cards.title: Misconception: Amdahl says big machines are pointless
cards.body: Amdahl’s law fixes the problem size. Gustafson’s observation is that people usually grow the problem with the machine: more data, finer models, more users. If the serial part stays roughly constant while the parallel part grows, more cores keep paying off. The useful question is whether your workload is a fixed task you want sooner, or a growing one you want to keep up with.

cards.title: Where serial time hides
cards.body: Serial work is not only code that runs on one thread. Reading an input file before splitting it, merging results at the end, waiting on one database connection, holding a global lock, or a single coordinator handing out tasks all count. Measure how the job’s time splits before parallelising, and shrink the largest serial step first: halving a 10% serial part raises the ceiling from 10 to 20 times.

questions.prompt: A job is 90% parallel. What is the most speedup any number of cores can give it?

choices.label: About 9 times, the parallel share over the serial share
As much as the number of cores you add to the job
10 times, since 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) is the ceiling
About 1.1 times, the inverse of the parallel share

questions.explanation: The serial 10% always takes its full time, so the job can never finish faster than one tenth of the original: 10 times. Nine is the ratio of parallel to serial work, not the limit; unlimited scaling ignores the serial part; and 1 ÷ 0.9 is what you get by mixing up which share is serial.

questions.prompt: A batch job runs in 40 s on 8 cores and in 55 s on 32 cores. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: The serial part grew because more cores were added
Threads contend for a shared lock or hot cache line
Amdahl’s law predicts slowdowns past 8 cores
The operating system can schedule at most 8 threads

questions.explanation: Amdahl’s law only flattens the curve; a job getting slower with more cores means coordination costs grow with core count, usually a contended lock, atomic or cache line. The serial code itself did not change, Amdahl never predicts a slowdown, and schedulers run far more than 8 threads.

questions.prompt: Analytics runs over 10 times more data each year on 10 times more cores. Run time stays about the same. Which idea explains why scaling still pays off?

choices.label: The serial share shrinks as the parallel work grows
Amdahl’s ceiling rises in proportion to the core count
Cache misses fall as more data is processed in total
More cores lower the time spent in each serial step

questions.explanation: This is Gustafson’s scaled speedup: if serial work stays roughly fixed while parallel work grows with the data, the serial share falls and more cores stay useful. Amdahl’s ceiling depends on the serial share, not on cores; more data usually means more misses, not fewer; and serial steps by definition do not speed up with cores.

questions.prompt: A pipeline spends 20 s reading input on one thread and 80 s processing in parallel on 4 cores. Which change shortens it the most?

choices.label: Doubling to 8 cores for the processing step
Splitting the input read across 4 threads
Raising the priority of the processing threads
Running the processing on faster, single-core hardware

questions.explanation: Now: 20 + 80 ÷ 4 = 40 s. Eight cores give 20 + 10 = 30 s. A 4-way parallel read gives 5 + 20 = 25 s, assuming storage keeps up. Priority does not create CPU time on an otherwise idle machine, and one fast core loses the 4-way parallel step.

questions.prompt: A job is 80% parallel. What speedup do 4 cores give?
assumptions: The serial 20% does not speed up
Parallel work splits perfectly across cores
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the ceiling for this job is 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 times, and 4 cores already reach half of it, so another 4 cores add only about 1.1 times more (to 3.3).

questions.prompt: A nightly report takes 90 minutes and must finish in 45. Choose the change.
constraints: Profile: 60 minutes reading files through one thread, 30 minutes of parallel scoring on 8 cores
Storage can serve about six times the current read rate
Budget allows a larger machine or a week of engineering

approaches.label: Parallelise the file reading
approaches.description: Split input reads across several threads or processes

approaches.label: Move to a 32-core machine
approaches.description: Quadruple the cores for the scoring step

approaches.label: Tune the scoring code for 20% gains
approaches.description: Optimise the parallel step’s inner loop

rationaleOptions.label: The 60-minute serial read alone is longer than the 45-minute budget
Storage headroom means a 6-way read could take about 10 minutes
Quadrupling the cores quarters the whole run time
Faster scoring code fixes the serial bottleneck

rationaleConflicts.r3: Only the scoring step speeds up: 60 + 30 ÷ 4 = 67.5 minutes, still over budget.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Scoring is the parallel part; 20% off it gives 60 + 24 = 84 minutes.

questions.explanation: With a 6-way read the job takes about 10 + 30 = 40 minutes, inside the target with no new hardware, while 32 cores still leave it at 67.5. When the serial part is the biggest slice, attack it first.

flashcards.back: Speedup = 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ N); ceiling 1 ÷ (1 − p).

flashcards.front: Why can more cores make a job slower?
flashcards.back: Coordination costs (locks, shared lines) grow with cores and can outweigh the extra work done.
Grow the problem with the machine; a fixed serial part becomes a smaller share.

sources.title: Amdahl, Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities (1967)

mechanism.title: Where parallel speedup goes
steps: Split the job’s single-core time T into a serial part s × T and a parallel part p × T, with s + p = 1.
On N cores the parallel part ideally takes p × T ÷ N while the serial part still takes s × T, so the run time is T × (s + p ÷ N) and the speedup is 1 ÷ (s + p ÷ N).
As N grows, p ÷ N approaches zero and the speedup approaches 1 ÷ s. Half the ceiling is reached at N = p ÷ s cores (19 cores for 95% parallel); after that each extra core buys less.

Real systems add a coordination cost that grows with N: threads queue for locks, cores fight over cache lines, and coordinators hand out work one task at a time. Models such as the universal scalability law add these terms, and they make throughput peak and then fall.
Gustafson’s scaled speedup holds run time fixed instead of problem size. If the serial part stays constant while parallel work grows with N, the speedup is about s + p × N, which keeps growing.
In practice, profile the split first, shrink the largest serial step (I/O, merging, global locks), remove shared hot spots, and only then add cores, measuring throughput at each size.

useWhen: Use Amdahl’s law to estimate the ceiling before buying cores or rewriting for parallelism.
Use it to rank optimisations: shrinking serial work raises the ceiling itself.
avoidWhen: Avoid scaling up a job that slows down as cores are added; find the contention first.
Avoid assuming linear speedup in capacity plans.

rows: Parallel share is large and cores are idle-free
Serial share is already a large slice
Time rises as cores are added

numbers.title: Is 4 times the cores worth it?
assumptions: A job is 95% parallel (illustrative)
Cost is proportional to cores × run time
steps: Speed gain: 12.55 ÷ 5.93 ≈ 2.1 times for 4 times the cores.
Cost per job: 2.55 ÷ 1.35 ≈ 1.89 times higher.
numbers.result: Quadrupling cores for a 95% parallel job gives about 2.1 times the speed at about 1.9 times the cost per job; halving the 5% serial part instead would raise the 32-core speedup to about 18.

india.title: Where the law comes from
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Gene Amdahl presented the argument in 1967 at the AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, in a paper titled “Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities”, arguing that a fixed share of sequential housekeeping work limits what parallel hardware can deliver. In 1988 John Gustafson’s “Reevaluating Amdahl’s law” in Communications of the ACM argued that in practice the problem size grows with the machine, so measured speedups on large parallel computers can far exceed the fixed-size prediction.

pitfalls.trap: “Doubling cores will halve the run time.”
pitfalls.say: “Only the parallel part halves; I’d measure the serial share and compute the real speedup.”

pitfalls.trap: “More cores made it slower, so the machine is bad.”
pitfalls.say: “That points to contention; I’d profile locks and shared state before scaling.”

takeaways: Speedup is capped at 1 ÷ serial share.
Each doubling of cores buys less than the last.
Contention can make extra cores slow a job down.
Shrinking serial work raises the ceiling; more cores never do.

interactive.title: Is triple the cores worth it?
interactive.prompt: A job has 10 s of serial setup and 90 s of perfectly parallel work when run on one core. You can run it on 10 cores or on 30.

choices.label: About 1.5 times faster: 19 s on 10 cores becomes 13 s on 30
About 3 times faster, because the cores triple
choices.feedback: Only the 90 s parallel part speeds up; the 10 s setup stays.

choices.label: No faster at all, because the setup dominates
choices.feedback: Setup is 10 s of the 19 s, so the parallel part still shrinks from 9 s to 3 s.

interactive.reveal: Triple the hardware buys 19 ÷ 13 ≈ 1.46 times the speed. Cutting the setup from 10 s to 5 s on 10 cores gives 14 s, almost as fast as 30 cores, without any new hardware.

seeAlso.why: Scheduling decides how threads share the cores in the formula
Locks are the most common source of serial time
Capacity plans should not assume linear scaling

title: Green Threads, Coroutines and Async Runtimes
objectives: Explain how a runtime multiplexes many lightweight tasks onto a few OS threads
Compare stackful and stackless designs and what each costs
Spot the calls that block a carrier thread and stall unrelated tasks

cards.title: Many tasks, few kernel threads
cards.body: Kernel threads are scheduled by the operating system and each reserves its own stack, so a process with tens of thousands of them pays for memory and context switches. Lightweight tasks (green threads, virtual threads, coroutines) are scheduled by a runtime in user space instead: it runs many tasks on a small pool of OS threads, called carriers, and switches between tasks when one waits for I/O, timers or a channel. This is M:N scheduling.

cards.title: Stackful or stackless
cards.body: A stackful task has its own small, growable stack, so it can pause anywhere inside ordinary nested calls and code looks blocking. A stackless coroutine is compiled into a state machine that saves only the variables live across each suspension point; it can pause only where the code marks a suspension (an await), and every caller up the chain must be async too. Stackless tasks are usually smaller; stackful ones avoid splitting the code into two colours.

cards.title: Worked example: one blocking call stalls everyone
cards.body: Four carrier threads run 10,000 tasks.
steps: A task calls a file or DNS function that blocks in the kernel instead of yielding to the runtime
Its carrier thread is now stuck in the kernel and cannot run any other task
If four tasks do this at once, all four carriers are blocked and 9,996 ready tasks wait, even though the CPU is idle
Latency spikes for unrelated requests until a blocking call returns
Fix: use the runtime’s non-blocking version, or hand blocking work to a separate pool sized for it

cards.title: Trap: holding a lock across a suspension point
cards.body: A task takes an ordinary mutex, then awaits a network call while holding it. The task is suspended, but the lock stays held, and another task on the same carrier that wants it blocks the carrier itself, which can deadlock a single-threaded runtime. Some runtimes also pin a lightweight task to its carrier while it holds a monitor lock. Release locks before suspending, or use a lock provided by the runtime that suspends instead of blocking.

cards.title: Misconception: lightweight tasks make CPU work faster
cards.body: Lightweight tasks make waiting cheap, not computing. A hundred thousand tasks each waiting on a socket cost little, but CPU-bound tasks still need cores, and a task that computes for 200 ms without reaching a suspension point delays every other task on its carrier in runtimes that switch only cooperatively. Move long computation to a worker pool sized to the core count, or yield periodically.

questions.prompt: A server handles 50,000 mostly idle connections. Why do lightweight tasks suit it better than one kernel thread per connection?

choices.label: The kernel runs lightweight tasks at a higher priority
Each waiting task costs a few kilobytes, not a full thread stack
Lightweight tasks run on more cores than the machine has
Lightweight tasks skip the system calls that I/O needs

questions.explanation: A suspended task keeps only a small stack or state machine and no kernel thread, so idle connections are cheap and the runtime avoids kernel context switches. The kernel does not see tasks at all, so it gives them no priority; they cannot use more cores than exist; and I/O still goes through system calls, just non-blocking ones.

questions.prompt: A service on an async runtime with 4 carrier threads stalls for seconds at a time while CPU stays low. Each stall coincides with slow responses from a legacy file share. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The runtime’s scheduler has too many tasks in its queue
The file share answers slowly, so the network stack retries
The runtime switches tasks too often, wasting time
Blocking file reads tie up all four carrier threads

questions.explanation: Calls that block in the kernel hold the carrier, and four slow reads at once leave no carrier free, so everything stops while the CPU idles. Long queues are normal and cheap, retries would show up as network errors rather than total stalls, and task switching is fast and would raise CPU, not lower it.

questions.prompt: A team moves from stackless coroutines to stackful virtual threads. What do they gain?

choices.label: Ordinary blocking-style code can suspend inside nested calls
Each task uses less memory than a stackless state machine
Tasks can now run CPU-bound work faster than before
The kernel can schedule each task directly on a core

questions.explanation: A stackful task saves its whole stack, so any function can suspend without marking every caller async. Stackless state machines are usually smaller, not larger; CPU-bound work runs at the same speed; and the kernel still schedules carriers, not tasks.

questions.prompt: On a single-threaded cooperative runtime, one request handler resizes an image for 300 ms without any await. What do other requests see?

choices.label: Nothing, because each task runs on a separate core
A small slowdown spread evenly across all tasks
A stall of up to 300 ms, since nothing else can run
An error, because the runtime cancels long-running tasks

questions.explanation: Cooperative runtimes switch only at suspension points, so a 300 ms computation holds the only carrier for 300 ms. Tasks do not get their own cores, the delay is not spread out because there is no preemption, and runtimes do not cancel tasks for running long.

questions.prompt: A server keeps 100,000 lightweight tasks alive, each using about 4 KB of stack or state. Roughly how many megabytes do they take?
assumptions: 1 MB is about 1,000 KB here
Only task stacks or state are counted
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same 100,000 connections on kernel threads with 64 KB committed each (illustrative) would need about 6.4 GB, sixteen times more, before counting context-switch costs.

questions.prompt: Order what a runtime does when a task reads from a socket that has no data yet.

items.label: The carrier thread picks the next ready task and runs it
The task calls the runtime’s read, which tries a non-blocking read and gets “would block”
When the event queue reports the socket readable, the task is made ready and later resumed
The runtime registers the socket with the event queue and suspends the task

questions.explanation: Try, park, run something else, resume on readiness: the carrier never sleeps while other tasks are ready.

flashcards.back: Many user-space tasks multiplexed by a runtime onto a few OS (carrier) threads.
Stackful: own growable stack, suspend anywhere. Stackless: state machine, suspend only at marked awaits.
Blocking system calls, long CPU work without yielding, or locks held across a suspension.

mechanism.title: How a runtime multiplexes tasks
steps: The runtime starts a pool of carrier threads, often one per core, each with a run queue of ready tasks. Idle carriers can steal tasks from busy ones to balance load.
A task runs on a carrier until it reaches a suspension point: an I/O call that would block, a timer, a channel or lock operation, or an explicit yield.

At a suspension, the runtime saves the task’s state (its small stack, or the state machine’s fields), registers interest with the kernel’s readiness mechanism such as epoll, and moves on to the next ready task on the same carrier.
One or more poller threads wait on the event queue. When a socket becomes readable or a timer fires, the matching task is put back on a run queue.
Calls the runtime cannot make non-blocking, such as some file system operations or name lookups, are passed to a separate blocking pool, or the runtime adds a carrier temporarily to compensate.

Some runtimes can preempt a task that runs too long; others are purely cooperative. In either case, code that blocks the carrier inside the kernel, or holds it through a lock, removes that carrier from service for everyone.

useWhen: Use lightweight tasks for many concurrent, mostly waiting operations such as connections and calls to other services.
Use a separate pool sized to the cores for CPU-heavy work.
avoidWhen: Avoid blocking system calls on carrier threads.
Avoid holding ordinary locks across a suspension point.

rows: Tens of KB to MB of stack
Memory and context switches at high counts
Blocking or pinned calls stall carriers

numbers.title: What a blocked carrier costs
assumptions: 4 carrier threads serving 1,500 requests a second at 2 ms of CPU each (illustrative)
A 1% minority of requests calls a blocking lookup that takes 100 ms
steps: CPU needed: 1,500 × 2 ms = 3 CPU-seconds per second, 75% of four carriers.
Blocking time: 1,500 × 1% × 100 ms = 1.5 carrier-seconds per second spent stuck in the kernel.
Demand on carriers becomes 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 carrier-seconds per second against 4 available, 112% of capacity, so queues grow without bound.
Moving the lookups to a separate blocking pool takes the carriers back to 3 of 4, 75% busy, and the queues drain.
numbers.result: A blocking call on just 1% of requests pushes the carriers from 75% to 112% of capacity here; keep blocking work off carriers.

india.title: How one runtime documents pinning
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Oracle’s documentation for Java virtual threads explains that a virtual thread is mounted on a platform carrier thread and unmounted when it blocks, freeing the carrier to run another virtual thread. It cannot be unmounted while pinned: when it runs code inside a synchronized block or method, or runs a native method or foreign function. The documentation notes that pinning does not make an application incorrect but can hinder scalability.

pitfalls.trap: “We switched to async, so it scales now.”
pitfalls.say: “Waiting got cheap; I’d still check for blocking calls and long CPU work on the carriers.”

pitfalls.trap: “A mutex is fine inside an async function.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if it’s released before any await; otherwise I’d use the runtime’s async lock.”

takeaways: A runtime runs many tasks on a few carrier threads.
Stackful tasks suspend anywhere; stackless ones only at awaits.
Blocking calls and held locks stall a carrier for every task on it.
Lightweight tasks make waiting cheap, not CPU work.

interactive.title: Why did the whole service freeze?
interactive.prompt: An async service runs on 2 carrier threads. Two requests arrive that each call a library function doing a blocking DNS lookup that takes 5 s because the resolver is down. Hundreds of other requests are queued.

choices.label: Both carriers are blocked in the kernel, so no task runs for 5 s
choices.feedback: Right: blocking calls hold their carriers, and only two exist.

choices.label: Only the two lookup requests wait; the others continue normally
choices.feedback: That would be true only if the lookups yielded to the runtime or ran on a separate pool.

choices.label: The runtime preempts the lookups after a time slice and moves on
choices.feedback: A thread blocked in a system call cannot be preempted by a user-space runtime.

interactive.reveal: Run blocking calls on a dedicated blocking pool or use a non-blocking resolver. Then the two lookups wait on their own threads while the carriers keep serving everyone else.

seeAlso.why: Event loops and readiness are the layer under every runtime
Choosing processes, threads or async I/O for a service
Kernel threads are what carrier threads are made of

title: Diagnosing a Slow Machine: Load, CPU Time and iowait
objectives: Check utilisation, saturation and errors for each resource in a fixed order
Read load average, CPU time categories and steal time correctly
Tell a CPU-bound, I/O-bound and memory-starved machine apart

cards.title: A checklist beats guessing
cards.body: For every resource (CPUs, memory, disks, network, and limits such as descriptors or a cgroup quota) ask three questions: how busy is it (utilisation), is work queuing for it (saturation), and is it reporting errors. Working through the list in the same order each time finds the bottleneck faster than staring at whichever graph looks worst, and it rules resources out as well as in.

cards.title: Misconception: load average is CPU usage
cards.body: On Linux the load average counts tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting for disk or a network file system), averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load of 16 on a 16-core machine can mean every core is busy, or that the CPUs are idle and 16 threads are stuck waiting for a slow disk. Compare load with core count and then look at CPU time categories before deciding which one it is.

cards.title: Worked example: three machines with a load of 12
cards.body: Same number, three different problems, on 8-core machines.
steps: Machine A: CPU 98% user time, run queue about 12: CPU-bound, four threads always waiting for a core
Machine B: CPU 85% idle and iowait, 10 threads in disk wait: I/O-bound, more cores would not help
Machine C: CPU 30% user, 40% steal: a virtual machine whose host is giving its CPU time to other tenants
Each needs a different fix: more CPU or less work for A, faster or fewer I/Os for B, a different host or instance size for C
The load average alone could not tell them apart; CPU categories and per-resource saturation could

cards.title: Trap: reading iowait as a busy CPU
cards.body: iowait is time a CPU sat idle while at least one task was waiting on disk I/O. It is idle time with a label, not work. High iowait means storage is the thing to look at, and it can drop to zero when an unrelated CPU-heavy job starts, even though the disk is just as slow. Check the disks’ own utilisation and queue length rather than trusting iowait’s size.

cards.title: Steal time and memory pressure
cards.body: On a virtual machine, steal time is time the guest wanted to run but the hypervisor ran something else; persistent steal means the instance is not getting the CPU it was sold or has used up burst credits. Memory problems look different again: little free memory is normal because of page cache, but rising major page faults, swap activity or reclaim stalls mean the working set no longer fits.

questions.prompt: A 16-core database server shows a load average of 20, but CPU is 80% idle. What is the most likely situation?

choices.label: The load counter is stale and should be ignored
Many threads are blocked waiting for disk I/O
Twenty processes are using a core at full speed
The server has more cores than the load can use

questions.explanation: Linux counts tasks in uninterruptible sleep, typically disk waits, in the load average, so a high load with idle CPUs points at storage. The counter is live, twenty CPU-bound processes would show the CPUs busy, and spare cores do not raise the load.

questions.prompt: A server’s iowait falls from 40% to 5% after a CPU-heavy batch job starts on it. Disk latency is unchanged. What happened?

choices.label: The batch job warmed the page cache, so disk waits stopped
The CPUs became fast enough to hide the disk latency
Idle time once labelled iowait is now used by the batch job
The kernel lowered the disk’s priority behind the CPU work

questions.explanation: iowait is idle CPU time while I/O is outstanding; once the CPUs have other work, that time becomes busy time instead, even though disk waits continue. A warmer cache would have reduced disk latency, faster CPUs do not change storage, and nothing reprioritised the disk.

questions.prompt: A virtual machine’s latency doubled overnight. Its own CPU usage is unchanged at 45%, but steal time rose from 1% to 30%. Which action addresses the cause?

choices.label: Tune the application’s thread pool size downward
Move to another host or a non-burstable instance type
Add swap so the guest can use more memory
Increase the guest’s disk read-ahead setting

questions.explanation: Steal time is CPU the hypervisor withheld, from noisy neighbours or exhausted burst credits, so the fix is outside the guest. Thread pool tuning, swap and disk read-ahead change nothing about how much CPU the host grants.

questions.prompt: A web host is slow. CPU is 35% busy with no throttling, disks are 5% busy, and memory shows 200 MB free of 32 GB, most of the rest as page cache. What should you check next?

choices.label: Network and limits such as descriptors and connection pools
Free memory, since 200 MB is dangerously low
The CPUs again, because 35% hides a saturated core
The disks again, because 5% is suspiciously low

questions.explanation: CPU, disk and memory look healthy: page cache is reclaimable, so low free memory is normal. Moving on to the remaining resources, network and software limits, is how the checklist works. A single saturated core is possible, but per-core figures would be checked as part of CPU, which showed no saturation here.

questions.prompt: A single-threaded process is pinned at 100% of one core on a 16-core machine. Roughly what overall CPU utilisation does the machine report?
assumptions: Nothing else is running
Overall utilisation is averaged across all cores
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a machine-wide 6% can hide a process that is completely CPU-bound, so check per-core and per-thread figures before calling the CPU idle.

questions.prompt: Choose the next step for a slow reporting server.
constraints: One disk at 100% utilisation with a queue of 30 requests

approaches.label: Investigate the disk workload
approaches.description: Find what issues the I/O and reduce or spread it

approaches.label: Raise the process priority
approaches.description: Give the reporting process more scheduler share

rationaleOptions.label: High load with mostly iowait means threads wait on storage
A saturated disk with a deep queue is the bottleneck
A load of 14 on 8 cores shows the CPUs are overloaded
More scheduler share speeds up waiting threads

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most of the load is threads in disk wait, and the CPUs are 80% idle or waiting.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Threads blocked on I/O are not waiting for a CPU, so priority does nothing for them.

questions.explanation: Every signal points at the disk: saturation (queue of 30), utilisation (100%) and load made of disk waits. Find the queries or jobs driving the I/O, add caching or indexes, or move to faster storage.

flashcards.back: For each resource check Utilisation, Saturation (queueing) and Errors.

flashcards.front: What does Linux load average count?
flashcards.back: Runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (often disk waits).
iowait: idle CPU while I/O is pending. Steal: time the hypervisor gave your vCPU to someone else.

mechanism.title: A repeatable pass over one slow machine
steps: Start with the symptom and the time it began, so later metrics can be compared with a normal period rather than judged in isolation.
CPU: overall and per-core utilisation; time split into user, system, iowait, steal and idle; run queue length or load against core count; and, in containers, throttled periods.
Memory: available memory (counting reclaimable cache), major page faults, swap in and out, and reclaim or pressure-stall figures. Low free memory alone is not a problem.
Disks: utilisation, queue depth and average latency per device. A device near 100% busy with a growing queue is saturated, whatever the CPU says.
Network: throughput against link capacity, retransmits and drops. Then software limits: descriptor counts, connection pools, thread pools and locks, which saturate without any hardware graph moving.
For each resource note utilisation, saturation and errors, move on when it is clean, and stop at the first resource that is saturated; then confirm by relieving it and watching the symptom.

useWhen: Use the same checklist on every incident so nothing is skipped under pressure.
Use CPU categories and per-device figures to explain a high load average.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating machine-wide CPU percentage as proof the CPU is fine.
Avoid reading low free memory or high iowait as the cause by itself.

rows: Available memory, swap and page faults

numbers.title: Reading one snapshot
assumptions: An 8-core VM over one minute: 0.9 runnable tasks per core on average, CPU time 40% user, 5% system, 15% iowait, 25% steal, 15% idle (illustrative)
steps: Runnable work: 0.9 × 8 ≈ 7 tasks, about one per core, so the run queue alone looks fine.
Work the guest got done: 40% + 5% = 45% of its CPU time.
Time it wanted but did not get: 25% steal, more than half as much again as the 45% of work actually done.
iowait of 15% is idle time; disks need checking, but steal is the larger loss.
numbers.result: Here a quarter of the VM’s CPU time is withheld by the host; fixing that (a different host or instance) is worth more than tuning the application.

india.title: Where the numbers come from
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The proc_loadavg(5) manual page describes the first three fields of /proc/loadavg as the number of jobs in the run queue (state R) or waiting for disk I/O (state D), averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. The proc_stat(5) page lists the CPU time categories in /proc/stat, including iowait, which it notes is not reliable, and steal, the time spent in other operating systems when running in a virtualised environment.

pitfalls.trap: “Load is 20, so we need more CPUs.”
pitfalls.say: “Load includes disk waits; I’d check CPU idle and disk queues before adding cores.”

pitfalls.trap: “Free memory is only 200 MB, we’re out of RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “Page cache is reclaimable; I’d look at available memory, swap and major faults.”

takeaways: Check utilisation, saturation and errors for every resource in order.
Linux load includes disk waits, not just CPU demand.
iowait is idle time; check the disks directly.
Steal time means the host, not your code, is taking the CPU.

interactive.title: What kind of slow is this?
interactive.prompt: A 4-core VM is slow. Load average is 4.2, CPU shows 50% user, 2% iowait, 45% steal and 3% idle. Disks are 10% busy.

choices.label: The host is withholding CPU from this VM
choices.feedback: Right: 45% steal means the guest wanted to run and the hypervisor did not let it.

choices.label: The application is CPU-bound and needs optimising
choices.feedback: User time is only 50%; nearly as much time is stolen as is used.

choices.label: The disk is saturated and threads wait for it
choices.feedback: iowait is 2% and disks are 10% busy, so storage is not the issue.

interactive.reveal: The load is about one per core and the guest is barely idle, yet half its CPU time is stolen. Moving to a dedicated or larger instance, or checking burst credits, addresses it; profiling the application would not.
