title: Memory-Mapped Files and Zero-Copy I/O
objectives: Explain how mapping a file differs from reading it into a buffer
Count the copies in a read-then-write path and what sendfile or splice remove
Know when mmap is the wrong tool, especially for databases and changing files

cards.title: A file that looks like memory
cards.body: mmap maps a range of a file into the process’s address space. Nothing is read at first; touching a page causes a page fault, and the kernel loads that page from the page cache, reading it from disk if needed. Reads and writes then go straight to page cache pages, with no read or write call and no copy into a private buffer. Several processes mapping the same file share the same physical pages.

cards.title: Worked example: counting copies when serving a file
cards.body: A server sends a 1 GB file to a client.
steps: Disk to page cache: done by the device with DMA, no CPU copy
read(): the CPU copies 1 GB from the page cache into the program’s buffer
write() to the socket: the CPU copies 1 GB from the buffer into socket buffers, then the network card sends it with DMA
Total: 2 GB of CPU copying and two system calls per chunk
sendfile(): the kernel moves page cache pages to the socket directly; no data passes through user space, and with gather-capable network cards no CPU copy remains

cards.title: Trap: a mapped file shrinks under you
cards.body: If another process truncates a file while you have it mapped, touching a page that is now past the end of the file raises SIGBUS, which by default kills the process. With read you would simply get a short read. Map only files you control, or that change by appending in a way you coordinate, and treat log files or user uploads that may be truncated as read-call territory.

cards.title: Misconception: mmap is always faster than read
cards.body: Each first touch of a page costs a page fault, and mapping, unmapping and updating page tables have their own costs, especially when many threads share the mapping. For one sequential pass over a large file, read with a large buffer often matches or beats mmap. mmap helps most for random access to data that stays hot and for sharing read-only data between processes.

cards.title: Why many databases avoid mmap for writes
cards.body: With a writable shared mapping, the kernel decides when dirty pages are written back, so the program cannot guarantee that its log reaches disk before the data pages it describes, which is the ordering crash recovery depends on. I/O errors arrive as signals rather than return codes, and page eviction is outside the program’s control. Engines that manage their own buffer pool and call write and fsync keep that control.

questions.prompt: A process maps a 10 GB file and reads 100 random pages from it. Roughly how much is read from disk, assuming nothing is cached?

choices.label: All 10 GB at the moment mmap is called
Only the pages touched, plus any read-ahead
Nothing, since mapped files live in RAM
Half the file, chosen by the kernel up front

questions.explanation: mmap only sets up the mapping; pages are loaded on first touch through page faults, and the kernel may read a little extra ahead. Nothing is loaded at map time, mapped data still comes from disk the first time, and there is no fixed share loaded up front.

questions.prompt: A file server uses read into a buffer and then write to the socket. CPU profiles show most time copying memory. What change removes those copies?

choices.label: Use a larger buffer so there are fewer read calls
Read the file with direct I/O to skip the page cache
Send from the page cache with sendfile or splice
Compress the file before writing it to the socket

questions.explanation: sendfile and splice move data from the page cache to the socket inside the kernel, so the two copies through user space disappear. A larger buffer reduces calls but not bytes copied, direct I/O still copies into the user buffer and then into the socket, and compression adds CPU work.

questions.prompt: A log indexer maps active log files. Occasionally it dies with SIGBUS right after the logs are rotated by truncation. Why?

choices.label: The mapped pages were reclaimed and could not be reloaded
The file grew past the size of the mapping it had created
Two processes mapped the file and corrupted each other
It touched pages past the new end of the truncated file

questions.explanation: Accessing a mapped page beyond the end of the file raises SIGBUS, and truncation moved the end. Clean pages are simply reloaded from the file when needed; growth past the mapping just leaves the new data unmapped; and shared mappings see the same pages consistently.

questions.prompt: Why do many database engines avoid writing their data files through a shared memory mapping?

choices.label: Mapped writes cannot be made durable with any call
The kernel chooses when dirty pages reach disk
Mapped files are limited to the size of physical memory
Writes through a mapping skip the page cache entirely

questions.explanation: Crash recovery needs the log to reach disk before the data pages it describes, and with a writable mapping the kernel can write back any dirty page at any time. Mapped writes can be flushed with msync; files larger than RAM can be mapped; and mapped writes go to page cache pages, they do not skip them.

questions.prompt: A server sends 2 GB/s of files using read and write. Roughly how many GB/s of CPU memory copying does switching to sendfile remove, assuming a gather-capable network card?
assumptions: Disk and network transfers use DMA, not the CPU
read and write each copy every byte once
questions.explanation: Sanity check: at roughly 5 to 10 GB/s of copy bandwidth per core (illustrative), 4 GB/s is about half a core or more, plus extra cache pollution, which is why file servers and proxies use zero-copy paths.

questions.prompt: A server sends an uncached file to a client with read and then write. Put the movements of its bytes in order.

items.label: write copies them from that buffer into the socket’s send buffer
The disk controller transfers the bytes into the page cache by DMA
The network card fetches them from the send buffer by DMA
read copies them from the page cache into the program’s buffer

questions.explanation: Two DMA transfers and two CPU copies; sendfile keeps the bytes in the kernel and drops both CPU copies.

flashcards.back: Maps file pages into the address space; data is loaded on first touch via page faults.

flashcards.front: Copies in read + write to a socket?
flashcards.back: Two CPU copies through user space; sendfile or splice remove them.
Raised when touching a mapped page past the file’s current end, for example after truncation.

mechanism.title: What the kernel does for mapped and zero-copy I/O
steps: mmap creates a virtual memory area describing a file range and its permissions. No data moves and no physical pages are assigned yet.

On first access the CPU faults. The kernel finds the page in the page cache, or reads it from disk (often with read-ahead), then installs a page table entry pointing at that page-cache page and retries the instruction.

For shared mappings, writes dirty the page-cache page directly; the kernel’s write-back later writes it to disk, or msync forces it. Private mappings copy a page on its first write so changes stay in the process.
With read and write, the kernel copies between the page cache and a user buffer, and again into socket buffers. Each copy touches every byte through the CPU caches.

sendfile passes page-cache pages to the socket inside the kernel. With network cards that can gather from scattered pages, the card reads the data directly and the CPU never copies it; splice offers the same idea between pipes and other descriptors.

Zero-copy paths only work when the kernel can send the bytes as they are. If the application must transform them, such as encrypting TLS in user space or compressing, the data has to pass through user space, unless the kernel performs that work (for example kernel TLS).

useWhen: Use mmap for random reads of large, stable files and for sharing read-only data between processes.
Use sendfile or splice for serving unchanged file bytes to sockets.
avoidWhen: Avoid mmap for files that other processes may truncate.
Avoid writable mappings where you must control the order of writes to disk.

rows: Small files or data that must change

numbers.title: Copy cost at file-server scale
assumptions: A server sends 1.25 GB/s, a 10 Gbit/s link at full rate (illustrative)
About 8 GB/s of memory copy per core (illustrative)
steps: read + write: 2 copies × 1.25 GB/s = 2.5 GB/s of CPU copying.
At 8 GB/s per core that is 2.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.31 of a core, before counting system calls and cache misses.
With sendfile and a gather-capable card: 0 GB/s of CPU copying, leaving system call and TCP costs.
At 100 Gbit/s (12.5 GB/s) the read + write path would need 25 GB/s of copying, about 3 cores just moving bytes.
numbers.result: Zero-copy saves about a third of a core at 10 Gbit/s and about three cores at 100 Gbit/s in this example; the faster the link, the more it matters.

india.title: What the manual pages promise
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The sendfile(2) manual page states that because the copying is done within the kernel, sendfile is more efficient than the combination of read and write, which would require transferring data to and from user space. The mmap(2) page lists SIGBUS for an attempted access to a page of the buffer that lies beyond the end of the mapped file, and SIGSEGV for a write into a region mapped read-only, the two signals a mapped-file reader must be prepared for.

pitfalls.trap: “mmap is zero-copy, so it’s always fastest.”
pitfalls.say: “It saves a copy but adds page faults; for one sequential pass I’d benchmark read with a large buffer.”

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s mmap the data file and let the OS handle durability.”
pitfalls.say: “The kernel picks the write-back order; I’d keep a log written with write and fsync.”

takeaways: mmap loads pages on first touch and shares them with the page cache.
read + write costs two CPU copies; sendfile can cost none.
Truncating a mapped file turns accesses into SIGBUS.
Writable mappings give up control of write-back order.

interactive.title: Which path for a static file server?
interactive.prompt: A server sends large, unchanging video files over plain HTTP at 40 Gbit/s and is CPU-bound. Profiles show time in memory copies and system calls.

choices.label: Send each file with sendfile so the bytes never enter user space
choices.feedback: Right: the kernel hands page-cache pages to the socket with no user-space copies.

choices.label: Map each file and write from the mapping to the socket
choices.feedback: This removes one copy, but the copy into socket buffers remains and page faults are added.

choices.label: Read with a 16 MB buffer to cut the number of system calls
choices.feedback: Fewer calls, but both copies of every byte remain.

interactive.reveal: At 40 Gbit/s (5 GB/s) read + write copies 10 GB/s, more than a core of pure copying. sendfile removes it; if the files must be encrypted, kernel TLS keeps the zero-copy path where the platform supports it.
